title: No evidence of multiple paternity in the purple crab Homalaspis plana (H. Milne Edwards, 1834) (Decapoda: Brachyura: Platyxanthidae)
content:
Abstract
Studying reproductive traits such as paternity is a central topic in evolutionary biology. Paternity patterns in decapod crustaceans are highly variable, with multiple paternity widely reported across the group. We evaluated the paternity pattern in the purple crab Homalaspis plana (H. Milne Edwards, 1834) (Brachyura: Platyxanthidae) by analyzing six microsatellite loci in 15 ovigerous females and their respective broods. Genotyping revealed a maximum of two non-maternal alleles per brood. No evidence of multiple paternity was detected, and all examined broods were consistent with single paternity under the resolution provided by the six microsatellite loci and pooled-progeny design. Because allele sharing between maternal and paternal genotypes can render some loci uninformative, particularly when detecting a low-frequency secondary sire, the results do not exclude cryptic multiple paternity below the detection resolution of the present dataset. To our knowledge, this is the first genetic assessment of brood paternity in a member of Platyxanthidae. The observed pattern may be associated with the exceptionally high male investment in seminal material and the formation of a massive internal sperm plug that occupies most of the female seminal receptacle, potentially restricting subsequent inseminations or the effective use of additional ejaculates. Although the study was based on pooled offspring and females collected from a single locality, the consistency of the multilocus results across all broods provides the first evidence that single paternity may be a predominant reproductive pattern in this population. Individual-offspring genotyping with a larger panel of highly polymorphic markers will be needed to exclude low-frequency, genetically cryptic secondary paternity. These findings provide new insights into the reproductive biology of H. plana and establish a basis for evaluating the potential effects of fishing-induced changes in population sex ratio and male abundance.
